why:
P3's data layer. A Room entity is a class and a table at once, and the graph has to hold both without confusing them: the id follows the declaration (`java:entity:shop.db.TopicEntity`) so it is unique and stable, while the **name** is the table (`topics`) so `data_layer_link` can reconcile it against a real `.sql` schema, which pairs entities by name. Every class here is therefore also a `Type` with its own `Field`s — the entity is a parallel view of the same declaration, the C#/PHP precedent, not a replacement for it. The case also pins the three edge sources that look alike and are not: a `ForeignKey(entity = X::class)` inside `@Entity` (REFERENCES), an `@Upsert` resolved through its *parameter type* (WRITES), and a `@Query` resolved by actually parsing the SQL — including a `DELETE` written as a raw string, which is a WRITES and not a READS.

#394 adds a fourth: `insertMystery`'s parameter type, `MysteryThing`, is declared *nowhere* in this tree — not even as a plain class. A write parameter is a class, never a table name, and provenance settles that regardless of whether the class happens to be declared somewhere: no `Entity` node, no `WRITES` edge, silence rather than a node named with a dotted class FQN.

#397 adds a fifth: `insertWild`'s parameter type, `WildEntity`, is a genuine `@Entity` declared in `shop.wild` and reachable from `shop.db` only through `import shop.wild.*` — no explicit import names it. `resolve` only ever tried a precise import or a same-package guess, never a wildcard prefix, so this used to be guessed into `shop.db` (where nothing declares it) and silently refused there — a recall miss, not a fabrication, but a miss on the most ordinary shape a wildcard import exists for.

The tiers of that lookup are pinned by two refusals rather than trusted. `Wild.kt` also declares an `@Entity` `MysteryThing` and an `@Entity` `WildDto`, both reachable through the same `import shop.wild.*`. `insertMystery` imports `com.vendor.MysteryThing` explicitly, and `insertDto` takes the plain `shop.db.WildDto` declared in its own package. Kotlin resolves an explicit import first, then the same package, then a star import, so neither parameter is the wildcard entity. A resolver that treated the tiers as peers found exactly one grounded `@Entity` among the candidates in each case and wrote to it: an invented `WRITES`, caught in review of #397.

refusals.why: PREDICTED BEFORE SCORING. `remove` is a `@Query` whose body is `DELETE FROM topics WHERE id = :id`. A reader that pattern-matched a table name out of the annotation — or that treated every `@Query` as a read because the word is 'query' — would call this a READS. It is a WRITES, and only parsing the statement tells you so. The same raw-string `"""` spelling is what 8 of the 18 @Query bodies in the validation app use.

PREDICTED BEFORE SCORING (#394). `insertMystery`'s parameter type, `MysteryThing`, is declared nowhere in this tree. A write parameter is a class, never a table name — the id built from it must never reach the unknown-table external-placeholder path, whether or not the class is declared somewhere else. Silence is the honest answer; an `Entity` named with a dotted class FQN is not a table name at anything.

PREDICTED BEFORE SCORING. `import com.vendor.MysteryThing` names the parameter's type outright, so `import shop.wild.*` is never consulted for it, although `shop.wild` does declare an `@Entity MysteryThing`. An explicit import is not a peer of a star import.

PREDICTED BEFORE SCORING, and it was happening on the #397 branch. `WildDto` is declared in `shop.db` itself, as a plain class, and a same-package type hides a star import whether or not it is an entity. The only `@Entity WildDto` is the wildcard one, so a resolver that counted grounded entities across both tiers found exactly one and wrote to it.

excluded: `insertMystery`'s parameter type resolves to nothing: no `Entity` node and no `WRITES` edge for it, by the refusal above. `MysteryThing` is now *imported* from `com.vendor` rather than named bare, which is what makes the fixture compile (#389) and also the realistic shape — a DAO taking a DTO from a dependency, rather than a typo. It stays external either way: the point is that nothing in this repository declares it, not how the name was written.
The seven `java:androidx.room.*` import targets are external, so they stay out of the node ratio per the rule in corpus/README.md; the IMPORTS edges to them still count.

READS/WRITES require the `sql` extra — `@Query` bodies are parsed with sqlglot, never regexed. Without the extra those two edges (`all`'s READS and `remove`'s WRITES) are absent by design and the case scores lower rather than the extractor guessing.
`import shop.wild.*` gets no `IMPORTS` edge: a star import names no single symbol, so there is no target to point it at. `ktor_routes` and `spring_routes` record their wildcards the same way.

A write parameter ambiguous across two star imports is not in this fixture, because Kotlin rejects that ambiguity at compile time and every fixture here compiles. It is pinned in `tests/pkg/test_kotlin_room.py` instead.
